transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-09-15
Start time: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Recording ID: ff-20250915-8347
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Ravi (Redwood Solutions), Tom (Pioneer InfoSec), Aisha (Pioneer Platform), Diego (Compliance), Jenny (SRE)

Summary:
Quick security/compliance review focused on what admin and audit events Redwood captures, how those events can be exported to a customer's SIEM/landing zone, retention knobs and encryption/KMS options for exported data. Agreed to follow up with SOC2 artifacts, sample schema, and a bench for high-volume export testing.

Topics covered:
- Event taxonomy: admin actions, API keys, token ops, role changes, console logins, service-to-service auth
- Export sinks: S3, GCS, Kafka, Splunk HTTP Event Collector (HEC), direct SIEM integrations
- Retention and legal holds, TTL vs cold storage, segmentation by tenant
- Encryption at rest in transit and customer-managed KMS keys for export buckets
- RBAC/SSO logging surface and how to map to customer identity (SCIM/SAML)
- Audit streaming performance and ordering guarantees

Action items (recorded in call):
- Maya to share SOC 2 Type II and ISO scope summary + DPA link
- Liam to produce export config examples for S3 + Kafka and suggested partitioning for 1TB/day
- Tom to send 'must-have' event list for compliance ingest

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: All right hey everyone thanks for joining, I think we have about 45 minutes, um today this is just a focused review on admin/audit logging and export options so we can make sure Pioneer has what you need for compliance and your SIEM ingest.
[00:14] Tom: Yep thanks, I think the big questions for us are what events are captured by default, is there any PII in those events, and how do we export them into our Splunk pipeline without losing ordering.
[00:28] Liam: Great, I can walk through the event classes first — apologies if I mangle any names, this is live transcribe — so we capture admin actions (user creation, role changes, policy edits), auth events (console, token exchange), key ops (KMS usage, rotation requests), and system-level operational events (node restarts, autoscale decisions).
[00:46] Aisha: When you say auth events does that include SAML assertions or just the success/failure?
[00:52] Liam: Mostly success/failure and the resulting session token issuance. We can include raw assertion IDs if the customer wants them; typically customers avoid exporting full SAML assertions to external sinks for privacy.
[01:10] Jenny: On the PII question — are usernames email addresses present? That's a deal for us because of residency rules.
[01:18] Maya: Good call — by default we include the actor identifier (username or service principal) and a hashed user id option. We can scrub or pseudonymize fields before export if you need that. That's configurable per-tenant.
[01:35] Diego: What about admin console actions that touch customer data, do those show object-level metadata?
[01:41] Liam: We include object identifiers and references but not full payloads. For example an export event would say 'export-job-123 kicked off for dataset X' but not include dataset contents.
[01:55] Tom: Ordering — if we ship to S3 and you have many events per second, what's the guarantee on ordering? We need monotonic ordering for certain audit trails.
[02:06] Liam: Good question. For S3 we write time-windowed files, we cannot guarantee strict event-level ordering across objects — we recommend Kafka or Kinesis for strict ordering with a partition key (like user_id or resource_id). For S3 we provide sequence tokens and chunk timestamps to reconstruct ordered streams if you replay them in order.
[02:28] Tom: OK that helps. And latency — if we use Kafka is it sub-second?
[02:33] Liam: When streaming to a Kafka cluster 99th percentile is usually under 500ms from capture to publish, depends on network and your broker topology. S3 is batched, typical delivery is 1-5 minutes depending on batch window.
[02:48] Aisha: We want to land to our VPC in AWS using customer-managed KMS keys, is that supported?
[02:55] Maya: Yes, for Dedicated and Private deployments you can provide KMS keys for the export bucket. For Hosted we support envelope encryption: we encrypt at rest with Redwood keys but we also support re-encryption when writing to your S3 with your CMK via cross-account role.
[03:12] Aisha: Cross-account role — is that recommended pattern?
[03:16] Liam: It's common — Redwood assumes a write role into your bucket, we rotate our write credentials, but the object is encrypted with your CMK. We document the IAM policy needed.
[03:27] Diego: How do you handle legal holds — we may need to keep an archive longer than normal retention.
[03:33] Maya: We support per-tenant retention configs plus legal hold flags. Legal holds convert retention to indefinite until released. For long-term we also support lifecycle transitions to Glacier/Coldline if you want cheaper storage.
[03:48] Tom: Are the exports signed and verifiable? We need a way to prove tamper-resistance for audit.
[03:54] Liam: We sign export manifest files with a service key and can provide per-file checksums. For high-assurance customers we recommend pushing to an append-only log (we support pushing to a ledger-like system or you can route through your own Kinesis with immutability policies).
[04:13] Jenny: What about RBAC changes — for example someone removes MFA requirement for a role, do you capture who made the change and the previous state?
[04:21] Liam: Yes, we capture actor, timestamp, before/after diff for policy-level changes. The diffs are kept in the audit events so you can see previous state. We limit the payload to diffs not full policies to reduce noise.
[04:37] Tom: On retention, what are default retention periods?
[04:41] Maya: Default hosted retention is 90 days for full events, 365 days for meta indexes. For Dedicated you can configure down to 30 days or up to indefinite depending on contract.
[04:52] Diego: Could we set different retention for admin vs system events? We want admin for 7 years but system logs for 1 year.
[04:58] Liam: Yes, retention is tiered by event class. You can set retention per-event-type and also route certain types to a separate long-term archive bucket with different lifecycle rules.
[05:12] Tom: Regarding format — is it JSONL? Avro? Protobuf?
[05:16] Liam: Default is JSONL for human readability, Avro or Parquet options are available for compactness at export time. We can generate schema registry entries if you want Avro.
[05:25] Aisha: Schema drift — if you change a field name in the application, how do we keep our ingest stable?
[05:30] Liam: We version event schemas. Each event includes schema_version and we retain older versions for x months. We can also emit a compatibility delta file to your sink when event schema changes.
[05:42] Maya: Quick note, there's a doc I'm going to share — the audit-export reference and the export policy templates, I'll attach those after the call. (link: https://redwood.ai/docs/audit-exports)
[05:55] Tom: Great, please include the example S3 bucket policy.
[05:59] Maya: Yep will do.
[06:02] Tom: One more — multi-tenant separation, do admin events include tenant id and do you ever fold events from different tenants into a single export stream?
[06:11] Liam: We always include tenant_id and we never intermix tenant events in a single file unless you specifically configure cross-tenant export which most customers don't. For cross-tenant admins (Redwood ops) those events are in a separate op-admin stream.
[06:26] Diego: For compliance we need raw timestamps correlated to UTC and to customer timezone — do you include both?
[06:32] Liam: We stamp events in UTC and include an optional local timezone field.
[06:38] Jenny: Any comprehensive list of event names we can drop into our SIEM mapping?
[06:42] Maya: We'll include a canonical event catalogue — Liam will link it in the follow-up.
[06:47] Tom: API keys and secrets rotation — are those exposures ever included in the logs?
[06:52] Liam: Secrets are redacted. We log the rotate/delete action and the key id but never the secret value. If a secret is accidentally logged by an app, we have scrubbing flows and a purge API but it's a manual process.
[07:06] Aisha: How do you authenticate the export process? Is it signed requests or IAM role only?
[07:12] Liam: For S3 we use an IAM role you own and a short-lived session token. For Kafka/Splunk we support mutual TLS or HMAC tokens depending on the sink.
[07:24] Tom: Can you push to Splunk HEC? We have Splunk Cloud.
[07:28] Liam: Yes, supported. We can batch and compress payloads and handle HEC token rotation. We have an example HEC auth flow in the export docs.
[07:37] Diego: Suppose we need to produce an audit trail for an incident report — how quickly can you pull historical events?
[07:44] Maya: Depends on retention and storage class. If events are in hot storage retrieval is immediate. If in Glacier or coldline retrieval may be hours. For incident response we recommend short-term hot copies or a read replica into your SIEM.
[07:59] Tom: Do you offer a streaming mirror into our VPC — like a secured pipeline?
[08:05] Liam: For Private deployments yes. For Hosted we can set up an egress tunnel to your VPC using a cross-account role and a private endpoint; bandwidth and egress costs apply.
[08:17] Aisha: Network-level — do you sign and encrypt in transit? TLS obviously, but do you support client certs?
[08:22] Liam: Yes TLS + mTLS for Kafka or mutual TLS for HTTPS, client certs supported.
[08:29] Jenny: On monitoring the export job itself — do you expose metrics and alerts?
[08:33] Liam: We publish per-export metrics into Redwood Console: lag, error rates, last-success-timestamp, bytes/day. You can also push those metrics to Datadog or Prometheus via our monitoring export.
[08:46] Tom: Regarding chain of custody we might need signed manifests and a verification workflow. You mentioned a manifest file earlier, can that be gpg signed?
[08:55] Liam: We currently HMAC sign and provide checksums; GPG signing is not a built-in option but we can provide the manifest and you can run signatures on your end, or we can discuss custom signing for enterprise.
[09:09] Diego: For SOC 2 auditors, do you provide an export usage report showing who accessed the export configs and when?
[09:15] Maya: Yes, admin access logs for the export config UI and API are part of the audit trail. They are included in the export stream under admin-config events.
[09:27] Tom: Any known limitations or gotchas?
[09:30] Liam: A few: for extremely high throughput (multi TB/day) we recommend Dedicated with direct peering to avoid egress hotspots; second, S3 ordering caveat mentioned earlier; third, schema changes require coordination if you have strict Avro consumers.
[09:46] Aisha: Can we do a spike — 1TB/day ingest to our Kafka cluster and measure tail latency?
[09:52] Maya: Absolutely, Liam can prepare a plan. We'll need broker endpoints and partitioning plan from you.
[09:58] Tom: Ok last bit — retention proofing. Auditors sometimes ask for policy snapshots. Can you export retention policy versions?
[10:06] Liam: Yes, policy versioning is stored and exportable as part of the admin-config history.
[10:12] Maya: Alright, quick recap and next steps then.
[10:15] Maya: Action items are in the notes: I'll send SOC2 + ISO summary, Liam will prep export config examples and bench plan, Tom will send required event list. We'll schedule the bench week of 9/22.
[10:28] Tom: Thanks everyone, that was useful.
[10:31] Maya: Thanks, I'll follow up with the attachments.
